name: Kingdom and its Cities
description: Meanwhile, the kingdom of K is getting ready for the marriage of the King's daughter. However, in order not to lose face in front of the relatives, the King should first finish reforms in his kingdom. As the King can not wait for his daughter's marriage, reforms must be finished as soon as possible. The kingdom currently consists of n cities. Cities are connected by n - 1 bidirectional road, such that one can get from any city to any other city. As the King had to save a lot, there is only one path between any two cities. What is the point of the reform? The key ministries of the state should be relocated to distinct cities (we call such cities important ). However, due to the fact that there is a high risk of an attack by barbarians it must be done carefully. The King has made several plans, each of which is described by a set of important cities, and now wonders what is the best plan. Barbarians can capture some of the cities that are not important (the important ones will have enough protection for sure), after that the captured city becomes impassable. In particular, an interesting feature of the plan is the minimum number of cities that the barbarians need to capture in order to make all the important cities isolated, that is, from all important cities it would be impossible to reach any other important city. Help the King to calculate this characteristic for each of his plan.
input_specification: The first line of the input contains integer n ( 1 ≤ n ≤ 100 000 ) — the number of cities in the kingdom. Each of the next n - 1 lines contains two distinct integers u i , v i ( 1 ≤ u i , v i ≤ n ) — the indices of the cities connected by the i -th road. It is guaranteed that you can get from any city to any other one moving only along the existing roads. The next line contains a single integer q ( 1 ≤ q ≤ 100 000 ) — the number of King's plans. Each of the next q lines looks as follows: first goes number k i — the number of important cities in the King's plan, ( 1 ≤ k i ≤ n ), then follow exactly k i space-separated pairwise distinct numbers from 1 to n — the numbers of important cities in this plan. The sum of all k i 's does't exceed 100 000 .
output_specification: For each plan print a single integer — the minimum number of cities that the barbarians need to capture, or print - 1 if all the barbarians' attempts to isolate important cities will not be effective.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 613D — Kingdom and its Cities [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
